name: Social Darwinism
info: Social Darwinism is a body of pseudoscientific theories that claim to apply evolution and survival of the fittest to society and politics; it arose in 19th-century Europe, is chiefly tied to Herbert Spencer, and fed eugenics, racism and imperialism.

facts.thinkers: Herbert Spencer, its chief developer, whose evolutionary theory was neo-Lamarckian; Thomas Malthus, whose 1798 population essay Spencer's work revived; Francis Galton, founder of eugenics; Ernst Haeckel, who ranked nine human species; William Graham Sumner, its American exponent; Yan Fu, who brought it to China; Alfred Rosenberg, a key proponent in Nazi Germany
facts.texts: Spencer's Progress: Its Law and Cause (1857), First Principles (1860) and The Social Organism (1860); Malthus's An Essay on the Principle of Population (1798); Galton's writings of 1865 and 1869; Sumner's What Social Classes Owe to Each Other (1883); Benjamin Kidd's Social Evolution (1894); Alexander Tille's Entwicklungsethik (1895); Richard Hofstadter's Social Darwinism in American Thought (1944)
facts.ideas: the strong should gain wealth and power and the weak lose them; struggle between individuals under laissez-faire capitalism; struggle between nations or races; eugenics and state-directed breeding; imperial expansion as a law of nature; opposition to aid for the poor; society as an organism that evolves; hereditary mental qualities
facts.today: Scientists generally consider it discredited as a theoretical framework, but it persists within popular culture; the term itself is used mostly by opponents, and scholars dispute whether it names any single coherent ideology

t: Social Darwinism claimed to apply biological evolution and survival of the fittest to society, but its leading exponent, Herbert Spencer, held neo-Lamarckian theories that predated and contradicted Darwin's.

Its forms ranged from defences of laissez-faire capitalism to racial and national struggle, eugenics, imperialism and fascism, so that The Concise Oxford Dictionary of Politics notes a social Darwinist could as well defend state socialism as laissez-faire.

Scholars link it to the Young Turks' campaigns against the Armenians and to Nazi Germany, including Aktion T4; its claims were largely discredited by the end of World War II, partly through that association and the scientific consensus against eugenics and scientific racism.
dyk: The phrase survival of the fittest was coined by Herbert Spencer, not Darwin, and Spencer was not described as a social Darwinist until the 1930s, long after his death; Richard Hofstadter made the term a standard shorthand in the United States in 1944.
ev: Spencer publishes Progress: Its Law and Cause, two years before Darwin's On the Origin of Species
Francis Galton puts forward the ideas later known as eugenics, and returns to them in 1869
The phrase social Darwinism first appears in print, in Joseph Fisher's article on landholding in Ireland, and Eduard Oscar Schmidt uses it at a conference in Munich
William Graham Sumner publishes What Social Classes Owe to Each Other
Peter Kropotkin publishes Mutual Aid: A Factor of Evolution, arguing that cooperation also serves natural selection
Chiang Kai-shek starts the New Life Movement, harking back to theories of social Darwinism
Richard Hofstadter publishes Social Darwinism in American Thought, which popularises the term in the United States

sections.origins:
The word Darwinism was coined by Thomas Henry Huxley in his March 1861 review of On the Origin of Species, and by the 1870s it described a range of concepts of evolution or development, without any specific commitment to Darwin's theory of natural selection. The phrase social Darwinism first appeared in Joseph Fisher's 1877 article on landholding in Ireland. One of its earliest uses for a social theory was by Eduard Oscar Schmidt of the University of Strasbourg at a conference in Munich in 1877, who noted that socialists, although opponents of Darwin's theory, used it to add force to their political arguments. An anarchist tract, Le darwinisme social by Émile Gautier, followed in Paris in 1880.

Theories of social and cultural evolution were common in Europe before Darwin. Enlightenment thinkers such as Hegel often argued that societies progressed through stages of increasing development, and earlier thinkers had stressed conflict as a feature of social life; Thomas Hobbes's 17th-century state of nature seems analogous to the competition for resources Darwin described. Social Darwinism differs from these theories in drawing Darwin's distinctive ideas from biology into social studies.

The ideas commonly given the label often predate the Origin. Herbert Spencer's Progress: Its Law and Cause appeared in 1857 and First Principles in 1860, and his thinking stemmed from his reading of Thomas Malthus. Spencer was not called a social Darwinist until the 1930s. Hofstadter's 1944 book made the term a standard shorthand for a complex of late-19th-century ideas.
sections.ideas:
Social Darwinism claims to apply the biological concepts of evolution and survival of the fittest to social class, economics and politics. Its proponents believe that the strong should see their wealth and power increase and the weak see theirs decrease,, but they define the strong and the weak differently. Many such views stress competition between individuals in laissez-faire capitalism; others stress struggle between national or racial groups and support eugenics, racism, imperialism or fascism.

Spencer supported laissez-faire capitalism on the Lamarckian belief that the struggle for survival spurred self-improvement which could be inherited. In The Social Organism (1860) he compared society to a living organism that evolves through processes analogous to natural selection. Malthus had argued in 1798 that a population outgrowing its food supply would see the weakest starve, and suggested that charity could worsen social problems. Francis Galton argued in 1865 and 1869 that mental qualities such as genius and talent were inherited like physical traits, and that heredity should become a conscious decision; in his view welfare and asylums let inferior people survive and reproduce faster than the superior. Neither Galton nor Darwin advocated policies restricting reproduction, because of their Whiggish distrust of government.

The simpler forms held that the poor should provide for themselves and receive no aid, though most early-20th-century social Darwinists supported better working conditions and salaries.
sections.spread:
In Germany social Darwinism took shape in the 1860s and 1870s in the exchange between Darwin and his German advocates August Schleicher, Max Müller and Ernst Haeckel. Haeckel read the evidence of languages as showing that nations were such distinct lines of evolution that mankind should be divided into nine species, and he built a hierarchy of them; Schleicher treated languages as species and applied competition to the spread of nations. Early German social evolution theory had an antiestablishment tone, setting progress against the alliance of throne and altar. Haeckel's Monist League was formed in 1904, and Friedrich von Hellwald popularised the ideas in Austria. After 1900 Alexander Tille's Entwicklungsethik (1895), which asked to move from Darwin to Nietzsche, turned the struggle for life into an aristocratic doctrine.

In Britain, the sociologist Benjamin Kidd used the notion in Social Evolution (1894) to account for what he called the Anglo-Saxon and Latin overflowing his boundaries, and it served to justify the New Imperialism. In the United States the ideas reached their greatest prominence in the Gilded Age. In Japan they entered from the late 19th century through Galton, Haeckel and Western eugenic studies, and in China through Yan Fu's translation of Huxley's Evolution and Ethics, to which he added national elements. By the 1920s the sociologist Pan Guangdan promoted eugenics in China.
sections.power:
Two regimes took up social Darwinist ideology. The Committee of Union and Progress of the Ottoman Empire, the Young Turks, adopted it; their belief in a life-or-death conflict between Turks and other ethnic groups motivated the genocides and ethnic cleansing carried out against the Armenians, and social Darwinism let them view the extermination of whole population groups, and the murder of women and children, as necessary and justified.

In Nazi Germany it became a major part of the ideology, combined with a similarly pseudoscientific theory of racial hierarchy that identified Germans as part of an Aryan or Nordic master race. Nazi propaganda films such as Alles Leben ist Kampf showed fighting beetles to illustrate survival of the fittest. Alfred Rosenberg was a key proponent. The same ideas helped advance mass murder through involuntary euthanasia, notably Aktion T4, which targeted mentally ill and disabled people. Because of the same belief that the weak should perish, the Nazis opposed social welfare, while retaining business competition and private property as economic engines. Hannah Arendt traced the path from social Darwinist ethics to racist ideology; scholars dispute whether Haeckel's Monist League led to the Nazis, since the Monists were freethinkers whose organisations the Nazis banned in 1933.

In Japan, social Darwinists used Arthur de Gobineau's three races to justify an imperialism that sought to civilise other peoples of the so-called yellow race.
sections.critiques:
Critics of the term say it is inconsistent. The Concise Oxford Dictionary of Politics observes that commitment to natural selection entailed nothing uniform for sociological method or political doctrine, so a social Darwinist could be a defender of laissez-faire or of state socialism, an imperialist or a domestic eugenist. The term has rarely been used by the ideas' own advocates and almost always pejoratively. The biologist Ernst Mayr called it a misnomer and preferred social Spencerism, because Spencer's theories were formed before Darwin's, rested on neo-Lamarckian inheritance and orthogenesis, and contradicted natural selection; Griet Vandermassen, Roberto Marchesini and Marco Celentano agree.

Creationists such as William Jennings Bryan argued that social Darwinism follows logically from Darwinism; biologists and historians, and academics such as Steven Pinker, answer that this is an appeal to nature, and most scholars hold it is not a necessary consequence of evolution. Darwin wrote that social instincts such as sympathy also evolved by natural selection, though some scholars argue his views came to incorporate those of Spencer. Peter Kropotkin argued in Mutual Aid (1902) that the fittest could be those who cooperate. Some argue that Rockefeller and Carnegie owed their rationale to social Darwinism, while Irvin G. Wyllie and Thomas C. Leonard argue that Gilded Age businessmen showed it little support.
sections.legacy:
Social Darwinism declined in popularity after World War I, and its purportedly scientific claims were largely discredited by the end of World War II, partly through its association with Nazism and partly through a growing scientific consensus that eugenics and scientific racism were unfounded. Haeckel's recapitulation theory, adopted by the emerging social sciences to cast non-European societies as “primitive”, has since been heavily refuted. Scientists generally consider social Darwinism discredited as a theoretical framework, but it persists within popular culture.

Later writers kept the vocabulary at work in other fields. Hofstadter, who used the term in the ideological war effort against fascism for a reactionary creed of competitive strife, racism and chauvinism, also devised the term Darwinist collectivism for the influence of evolutionary ideas on collectivist views; the Fabians of the early 1900s, for instance, sought to use the state to reconcile a form of state socialism and the reduction of poverty with eugenics policies. H. G. Wells was heavily influenced by Darwinist thought but reacted against social Darwinism, while Jack London wrote survival stories that incorporated his views on it.

It has also been claimed that commercial Darwinism operates in markets worldwide, pitting corporation against corporation. Scholars still debate how far the various social Darwinist ideologies reflect Darwin's own views on human social and economic issues.

summary: Social Darwinism is a body of pseudoscientific theories applying evolution and survival of the fittest to society, chiefly tied to Herbert Spencer. Its forms ran from laissez-faire to eugenics, racism and imperialism, and it fed the Young Turks' campaigns against the Armenians and Nazi ideology; scientists now consider it discredited.
references: Peter J. Bowler, Evolution: The History of an Idea (University of California Press, 2003)
Peter Dickens, Social Darwinism: Linking Evolutionary Thought to Social Theory (Open University Press, 2000)
Mike Hawkins, Social Darwinism in European and American Thought 1860–1945: Nature and Model and Nature as Threat (Cambridge University Press, 1997)
Richard Hofstadter, Social Darwinism in American Thought (University of Pennsylvania Press, 1992)
notes: Start 1857, circa true: Spencer's Progress: Its Law and Cause (1857) is the earliest dated work the article ties to the ideas; the article says the label commonly refers to ideas that predate the Origin, and the phrase itself first appears in 1877. End null: the article says it is discredited as a framework but persists in popular culture.

The article contradicts itself on the origin of the term: it says Émile Gautier coined it with reference to a health conference in Berlin in 1877, while the later section credits Eduard Oscar Schmidt with an early use at a conference in Munich in 1877 and Gautier with a Paris tract of 1880; it also says the term first appeared in Europe in 1879, and quotes Foner for the 1860s. I give only Fisher 1877, Schmidt at Munich 1877 and Gautier's 1880 tract, and omit the 1879 and 1860s dates.
The article gives no casualty figures for the Armenian genocide, Aktion T4 or the Holocaust; none are written. Nazism's 'Holocaust' is not named in the article, so it is not named here.

The lead says Spencer's evolutionary theories were neo-Lamarckian and 'predated and contradicted Darwin's'; Mayr's view is attributed to him, and Spencer's own phrase 'survival of the fittest' is stated by the article as coined by Spencer.
Galton: the article says he put forward eugenics in 1865 and 1869; 'founded eugenics towards the end of the 19th century' is also in the article. The 1865 event uses the first.

The article's 'on the basis of U.S. theory and practice, commercial Darwinism operates in markets worldwide' is unsourced; I report it as the article's claim only in the legacy section and the editor may cut it.

Left out: Nietzsche's long quotation, Kubrick, Churchill's remarks on the feebleminded (kept out as a single man's view), Bork's quotation, the Rockefeller quotation, Zhang Jingsheng, Kropotkin's long extracts, the Irish tenure passage, and the Dublin-review primary sources.
Rosenberg and Sumner are named by the article as key proponent and exponent; the article says contemporary historians doubt Sumner's belief.
